landscape: Policy data fall into two traditions. The first measures policy-making itself: what governments attend to (the Comparative Agendas Project and its national projects) and how policies spread (the State Policy Innovation and Diffusion database). It also covers how far outputs follow opinion (the Gilens representation data, state policy liberalism) and how organised interests take part (lobbying and interest-group datasets). This tradition is strongest for the United States, where the Correlates of State Policy and SPID support a large literature on state politics and diffusion.

The second tradition codes the content of policies across countries. Examples are social protection entitlements (SPIN, TaxBEN), social protection coverage in middle- and low-income countries (ILO, ASPIRE, SALMIC), family policy, employment protection and minimum wages. Others cover education systems, LGBTQ+ rights, drug policy, criminal justice and COVID-19 responses. These datasets come from academic teams (SPIN, CBR-LRI, EPSM, CoronaNet) and from international organisations (OECD, ILO, World Bank). The OECD sources are authoritative but limited to member countries, and several block automated access.

Of the 75 POLICY rows, 31 are frozen. These include the COVID-19 trackers, which ended in 2022, and several social-policy datasets built by single research projects. Spending-based welfare measures (OECD SOCX, CWED, CPDS) are must-include datasets for the political-economy domain and are catalogued there.

core.text: The Comparative Agendas Project codes bills, laws, hearings, executive speeches, budgets, party manifestos and media in about 20 countries into a common scheme of major and minor policy topics. The shared scheme allows governments' attention to be compared over time and across countries. Its master portal brings the national projects together. It measures salience, not policy direction, and topic coding depends on how national teams map local policies onto the master scheme.

The Correlates of State Policy Project merges more than 3,000 variables on the 50 U.S. states, roughly from 1900 to 2019, covering policies, politics, demographics and economics, into one state-year file with a codebook. Its single state-year file makes it a convenient starting point for quantitative state politics. As a compilation, its quality varies by source and many series are short or gappy.

The State Policy Innovation and Diffusion database records the first adoption of 724 policies by U.S. states, from 1691 to 2017, together with inferred diffusion networks and state innovativeness scores. It is widely used in policy-diffusion research. Its policy universe reflects what earlier scholars chose to track, and it records only first adoptions.

The Social Policy Indicators Database (Stockholm University) codes legislated social insurance and assistance entitlements for model households in 37 countries from 1930 onward. Its modules cover sickness, unemployment, pensions, family benefits, social assistance and more. It allows welfare generosity to be compared from the legislation side. It measures entitlements, not take-up or actual benefits.

The Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker coded containment, economic and health policies daily for 185 countries and many subnational units from January 2020 to December 2022, with composite stringency and response indices. It is widely used in research on pandemic policy. Its indices record the presence and strictness of measures rather than compliance.

choosing: Distinguish attention, adoption, content and outcomes. Agenda data show which issues governments address; adoption data (SPID) show when policies are enacted; entitlement and regulation indicators (SPIN, EPL) show what the rules say; spending and coverage data show what the rules deliver. Combining these levels is often where the research question lies.

For cross-national indicators, weigh coverage against comparability. OECD and SPIN data are carefully harmonised for rich democracies; ILO, World Bank and WORLD data cover most countries but rely on more heterogeneous national sources.
gaps: Cross-national data on policy adoption and diffusion outside the United States and Europe remain scarce; most diffusion datasets are U.S.-state based.
Systematic data on interest-group activity outside the United States and the EU are rare, and disclosure-based lobbying data miss informal influence.
Several sectoral datasets are single-project snapshots now frozen (family policy, minimum-wage institutions, social reforms), and some OECD and NGO sources are reachable only interactively.
